5.
Clean Ramsey conglomerates

Our goal in this section is to establish a version of
Proposition
2.6

not addressing distances and odd girth yet, but preserving
clean intersections and the clique number.
For that we define an adequate notion of clean intersections
for conglomerates.

Definition 5.1
.

Given a graph
F
and an
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with
clean intersections,
a
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
is said
to be
clean

provided that

(

)

the copies in
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}
have clean intersections;

(

)

for every
(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{B}
and
every
F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\smallsetminus{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}
the intersection
of
B^{\star}
and
F_{\star\star}
is clean;

(

)

and for all distinct
(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}),(B^{\star\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star\star}_{F})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{B}
the intersection
of
B^{\star}
and
B^{\star\star}
is either clean or a copy of
F

belonging to
{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}\cap{\mathscr{B}}^{\star\star}_{F}
.

The following proposition yields clean conglomerates that
preserve the clique number and
enjoy the Ramsey property for colouring copies of
F
.

Proposition 5.2
.

For every ordered
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with clean intersections
and every number of colours
r
there exists a clean
ordered
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
‡
‡

‡

The superscript
in
\varUpsilon^{(1)}_{r}
indicates it is the first member of
a family of constructions
\varUpsilon^{(n)}_{r}
defined in
§
6
.

\varUpsilon^{(1)}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})=(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})

such that
{\mathscr{H}}_{B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}
and
\omega(H)=\omega(B)
.

The proof involves two applications of the partite construction method.
In a first major step we obtain the so-called
clean
partite lemma
—an
improved version of the Hales–Jewett construction which yields clean
partite conglomerates (see Proposition
5.6
). Armed with this
result and utilising the well-known fact that ordered graphs and induced
embeddings form a Ramsey category (quoted as Theorem
5.8
below)
we can then derive Proposition
5.2
by means of a second
partite construction.

5.1.
Pictures

Before starting a partite construction, one needs to define
an appropriate
notion of pictures and clarify how they amalgamate. For
reasons that will become
apparent later, we need to work with a slightly relaxed
version of conglomerates
to this end.

For a fixed graph
F
, an
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
is said to
be a
semi-induced
subsystem
of another
F
-system
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
if
B
is an
induced subgraph of
H

and
{{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\subseteq{\mathscr{H}}_{F}}
. So in contrast to induced subsystems the
reverse inclusion
{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\supseteq{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\cap\binom{B}{F}
is
not necessarily satisfied.
Triples
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
such that
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
is an

F
-system and
{\mathscr{H}}_{B}

is a collection of semi-induced copies of
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
in

(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
will be referred
to as
weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerates
.

Definition 5.3
.

Suppose that
F
is a graph,
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
is an

F
-system, and
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})

is a weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate. A
picture
over

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})

is a triple
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
consisting of a

G
-partite graph
\Pi

and subsets
{\mathscr{P}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{\Pi}{F}
,

{\mathscr{P}}_{B}\subseteq\binom{(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{F})}{(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})}
such
that the projection

\psi\colon V(\Pi)\longrightarrow V(G)
sending each vertex class

V_{x}(\Pi)
to
x
maps
each copy in
{\mathscr{P}}_{F}
to a copy in
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
and each copy
in
{\mathscr{P}}_{B}
to a copy
in
{\mathscr{G}}_{B}
.

We would like to emphasise that the map
\psi
, called the

canonical projection

of
\Pi
, is uniquely determined by the
G
-partite structure of
\Pi
.
The vertex classes
V_{x}(\Pi)
of a picture are also called
its
music lines
.
In figures, they are usually drawn horizontally.
For each copy
{F_{\bullet}}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
we define the
constituent
of
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})

over
{F_{\bullet}}
to be the following partite
{F_{\bullet}}
-system

(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}})
.

•

The underlying graph of
\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}
is the subgraph of

\Pi
induced
by
\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{x\in V({F_{\bullet}})}V_{x}(\Pi)
and the vertex
classes determining
its
{F_{\bullet}}
-partite structure are the music lines
V_{x}(\Pi)
.

•

The set
{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}
consists of all members of

{\mathscr{P}}_{F}
projected
by
\psi
onto
{F_{\bullet}}
. Equivalently, we set

{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}=\{F_{\circ}\in{\mathscr{P}}_{F}\colon V(F_{\circ})\subseteq V(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}})\}
.

Notice that each copy in
{\mathscr{P}}_{F}
belongs to a unique
constituent, while vertices
and edges of
\Pi
can belong to many constituents.

The picture every partite construction begins with, called

picture zero
, can be
defined over every weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
.
This picture
(\Pi_{0},{\mathscr{P}}_{0,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{0,F})
is obtained
by taking vertex disjoint
copies of
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
, one for each member of
{\mathscr{G}}_{B}
, and
placing them onto
the music lines in such a way that the canonical projection

\psi_{0}
of
\Pi_{0}

sets up a bijection between the set
{\mathscr{P}}_{0,B}
of these
copies and
{\mathscr{G}}_{B}
.
As an
F
-system
(\Pi_{0},{\mathscr{P}}_{0,F})
is the disjoint union
of the
F
-systems
constituting
{\mathscr{P}}_{0,B}
. For clarity we point out that
picture zero satisfies

\displaystyle|V(\Pi_{0})|

\displaystyle=|V(B)|\cdot|{\mathscr{G}}_{B}|\,,

\displaystyle|E(\Pi_{0})|

\displaystyle=|E(B)|\cdot|{\mathscr{G}}_{B}|\,,

and

\displaystyle|{\mathscr{P}}_{0,B}|

\displaystyle=|{\mathscr{G}}_{B}|\,,

\displaystyle|{\mathscr{P}}_{0,F}|

\displaystyle=|{\mathscr{B}}_{F}|\cdot|{\mathscr{G}}_{B}|\,.

Given a picture
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
over a weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
, a copy
{F_{\bullet}}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
and a partite

(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}})
-conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F_{\bullet}})
we define
the picture

(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})=(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F_{\bullet}})

to be the result of the following amalgamation procedure.

•

Recall that each copy

(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}}
is a
partite
{F_{\bullet}}
-system isomorphic to the constituent

(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}})
of
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})

over
{F_{\bullet}}
. Thus each of these copies can be extended to a copy

(\Pi_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ})
of this
picture. We suppose that these
extensions are constructed as disjoint as possible, so that we have

V(\Pi_{\circ})\cap V(\Pi_{\circ\circ})=V(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ})\cap V(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ\circ})

for all distinct

(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ}),(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ\circ})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}}
.

•

As a graph,
\Sigma
is the union of
H
with all
graphs
\Pi_{\circ}
obtained
in this way. Moreover, the
G
-partite structure of

\Sigma
is defined by setting

V_{x}(\Sigma)=\begin{cases}\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\bigl\{V_{x}(\Pi_{\circ})\colon(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}}\bigr\}\,,&\text{ if }x\not\in V({F_{\bullet}})\cr V_{x}(H)\,,&\text{ if }x\in V({F_{\bullet}})\,.\end{cases}

•

Put

\displaystyle{\mathscr{Q}}_{F}

\displaystyle=\bigcup\bigl\{{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ}_{F}\colon(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}}\bigr\}\cup{\mathscr{H}}_{F_{\bullet}}

and

\displaystyle{\mathscr{Q}}_{B}

\displaystyle=\bigcup\bigl\{{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ}_{B}\colon(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ})\in{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}}\bigr\}\,.

It is straightforward to check that
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
is indeed a picture
over
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
. The copies
(\Pi_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ})

of the given picture
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
constructed in
the first bullet are
called the
standard copies
of
{(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})}

in
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
.

5.2.
The clean partite lemma

The partite conglomerates produced by the Hales–Jewett construction have
properties
( )
‣
5.1
and
( )
‣
5.1
of
Definition
5.1
, but
they are capable of violating
( )
‣
5.1
, so that they
are usually not
clean. Our first application of the partite construction method leads to
another partite lemma, which gives better control over the intersections
of two copies.

Let us point out that when we have a picture

(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
over a weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
,
then by “forgetting” the
G
-partite structure of
\Pi
we
can view this picture
as a
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate (which, however, by
Definition
5.3
cannot be “only a weak one”).
Accordingly, we can also speak of clean pictures.
For instance, picture zero is clean as soon as the copies in

{\mathscr{B}}_{F}
have clean
intersections.
Next we show that, under suitable assumptions,
which are satisfied
when
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
is obtained by means of the
Hales–Jewett construction,
being clean is preserved by partite amalgamations. This
observation can be traced back
to
[
2
]
*Lemma 2.12 (see also
[
29
]
*Lemma 4.5).

Lemma 5.4
.

Let
F
be a graph,
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
an
F
-system with clean
intersections,
and
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
a
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate such that

(
)

the copies in
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
have
clean intersections;

(
)

and for every
(B^{\prime},{\mathscr{B}}^{\prime}_{F})\in{\mathscr{G}}_{B}
and
every
F_{\star}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}\smallsetminus{\mathscr{B}}^{\prime}_{F}

the intersection of
B^{\prime}
and
F_{\star}
is clean.

If we have

(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})=(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{{F_{\bullet}}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}})

for two pictures
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
,
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
over

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
, the copies in
{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}}

have clean intersections,
and the picture
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
is clean, then so
is
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
.

Proof.

Stage A:

Let
\psi\colon V(\Sigma)\longrightarrow V(G)
be the canonical projection
of
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
. The following projection argument
will often be used implicitly.

Claim 5.5
.

Let
Z
be a subgraph of
\Sigma
that either belongs
to
{\mathscr{Q}}_{F}
or underlies a member of
{\mathscr{Q}}_{B}
.
If for some copy
F^{\prime}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
we have

V(F^{\prime})\not\subseteq\psi[V(Z)]
,
then the constituent of
\Sigma
over
F^{\prime}
has a clean
intersection with
Z
.

Proof.

By our assumptions
( )
‣
5.4

and
( )
‣
5.4
, the intersection
of the graphs
\psi[Z]
and
F^{\prime}
is clean, whence

\psi[V(Z)]\cap V(F^{\prime})
contains
at most two vertices, and if there are two, then they
form an edge of
\psi[Z]
.
Since
\psi|_{V(Z)}
is a graph isomorphism, this entails
our claim.
∎

We need to show that the new picture
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
satisfies

( )
‣
5.1
–
( )
‣
5.1
of Definition
5.1
.

Stage B:

Beginning with
( )
‣
5.1
, we consider two distinct

F_{\star},F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{Q}}_{F}
. If their

\psi[F_{\star}],\psi[F_{\star\star}]\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}

they have a clean intersection by

( )
‣
5.4
and, hence,
the intersection of
F_{\star}
,
F_{\star\star}
is clean. So we may assume

F^{\prime}=\psi[F_{\star}]=\psi[F_{\star\star}]
for some
{F^{\prime}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}}
from

is the copy over which the

we appeal to the assumption that the copies in

have clean

we
let
(\Pi_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ})
,

(\Pi_{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ\circ})

be the standard copies of
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})

satisfying
F_{\star}\in{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ}
and
F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ\circ}
,
respectively. If

our claim follows
from
{\mathscr{P}}_{F}

having clean intersections, so the interesting case is

\Pi_{\circ}\neq\Pi_{\circ\circ}
.
Now we have

V(F_{\star})\cap V(F_{\star\star})\subseteq V(\Pi_{\circ})\cap V(\Pi_{\circ\circ})\subseteq V(H)\,,

whence
\psi[V(F_{\star})\cap V(F_{\star\star})]\subseteq V(F^{\prime})\cap V({F_{\bullet}})
.
The clean intersections of

imply that

applied to

and

here in place

,
if

.

Stage C:

Continuing with

‣

and

is clean.
Let
{(B^{\prime},{\mathscr{B}}^{\prime}_{F})\in{\mathscr{G}}_{B}}

and

and

,

‣

and Claim

, so

First case:

and

Second case:

Now there are standard copies

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}_{F}^{\star})\in{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ}

In the special case

‣

of

.

Stage D:

Proceeding with part

‣
5.1
of

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})

in

and standard copies

(\Pi_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ})
,

(\Pi_{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}_{F}^{\circ\circ})

such that

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})\in{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ}

and

(B^{\star\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star\star}_{F})\in{\mathscr{P}}_{B}^{\circ\circ}
.
If these standard copies coincide, we just need to exploit
that

is clean.
So suppose
\Pi_{\circ}\neq\Pi_{\circ\circ}
from now on, which yields

Let
(B^{\prime},{\mathscr{B}}^{\prime}_{F})
and
(B^{\prime\prime},{\mathscr{B}}^{\prime\prime}_{F})
be the projections

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})
and
(B^{\star\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star\star}_{F})
in

.
In the special case

‣

shows that

.

So we can henceforth suppose

.
This means that there are copies

. So either

,
and thus a member of
{{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}\cap{\mathscr{B}}^{\star\star}_{F}}
.
This proves

‣
5.1
and, hence, the lemma.
∎

Suppose now that a graph
F
, a partite
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with clean intersections,
and a number of colours
r
are given. The partite
construction we have in mind produces a clean partite
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
with

{\mathscr{H}}_{B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}
. This conglomerate will be
denoted by
{\mathrm{CPL}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})}
,
where
\mathrm{CPL}
abbreviates “clean partite lemma”; it is
constructed as follows.

•

Set
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})=\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
and
enumerate
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}

arbitrarily as

{\mathscr{G}}_{F}=\{F(1),\dots,F(N)\}\,.

•

Starting with picture zero we recursively define a
sequence
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)_{\alpha\leq N}

of pictures over
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
. If for some

\alpha\in[N]
the
picture
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\bigr)
has just
been constructed, we subject its constituent over
F(\alpha)
to the
construction
{\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(\cdot)}
, thereby obtaining a conglomerate

\bigl(H_{\alpha},{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}\bigr)
,
and then we set

(5.1)

\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)=\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\bigr)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}\bigl(H_{\alpha},{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}\bigr)\,,

where the amalgamation occurs over
F(\alpha)
.

•

This recursive construction ends with a terminal

\bigl(\Pi_{N},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F}\bigr)
.
As
\Pi_{N}
is a
G
-partite graph, while
G
itself is an

-partite graph,

F
-partite structure on

by setting

V_{x}(\Pi_{N})=\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits\bigl\{V_{y}(\Pi_{N})\colon y\in V_{x}(G)\bigr\}

for every

.
Owing to the fact that
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
is a partite

-system, we can

{(\Pi_{N},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F})}
as a partite
F
-system as well. For a

as
a partite
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate. This partite conglomerate
will henceforth be denoted by

.

Proposition 5.6
.

For every graph
F
, every partite
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})

with clean intersections,
and every number of colours
r
the partite
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate

\mathrm{CPL}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})=(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})

is clean and satisfies

(
)

{\mathscr{H}}_{B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}
,

(
)

{\mathscr{H}}_{B}\subseteq\binom{H}{B}_{\mathrm{dp}}
,

(
)

\omega(H)=\omega(B)
,

(
)

as well as
\mathrm{og}(H)=\mathrm{og}(B)
.

Proof.

Clearly, picture zero is clean. Repeated applications of
Lemma
5.4

show that all pictures
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)

defined in the course of the partite construction are

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})

( )
‣
5.4

and
( )
‣
5.4
of Lemma

due to

.
Similarly, for every
\alpha\in[N]
the copies in the sets

{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}

appearing horizontally have clean intersections, provided
that in the previous picture
the copies in
{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}
have clean
intersections. In particular, the final
picture
\bigl(\Pi_{N},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F}\bigr)
and thus the

(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
is clean.

The partition relation
{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}

follows from a standard
argument in the area, so we shall be brief about it. The
main point is that an

\alpha\in\{0,1,\dots,N\}
discloses that

for every colouring
\varphi\colon{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\longrightarrow[r]

there is a copy

\bigl(\widetilde{\Pi}_{0},\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,B},\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,F}\bigr)
of
picture zero
in
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)

such that for every
{\beta\in[\alpha]}
the constituent
of
\bigl(\widetilde{\Pi}_{0},\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,B},\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,F}\bigr)

over
F(\beta)
is monochromatic
§
§

§

More precisely,
if
\bigl(\widetilde{\Pi}^{F(\beta)}_{0},\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,F}^{F(\beta)}\bigr)

denotes that constituent, we mean that all elements
of
\widetilde{{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,F}^{F(\beta)}
have the same colour.
.

This statement is vacuously true for

and in the

over

( )
‣

).

In particular, for

we learn that for every colouring

( )
‣
4.4
,
to the

-colouring

of

.
Thereby we find a monochromatic copy

.
Now, if
(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})

is

, which completes the proof of

‣

.

For the remaining three statements we need the canonical

.
Since

‣

and

‣

.

It remains to address

‣

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}_{F}^{\star})\in{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B}

connecting two vertices

y
of
B^{\star}
.
By Proposition
4.4
( )
‣
4.4

\psi

sends
B^{\star}
to
some
B^{\prime}\in\binom{G}{B}_{\mathrm{dp}}
. Thus there is a

\psi(x)
-
\psi(y)
-path
Q\subseteq B^{\prime}

whose length is at most the length of
P
. The graph
isomorphism
\psi|_{V(B^{\star})}

between
B^{\star}
and
B^{\prime}
allows us to pull
Q
back to
B^{\star}
.
∎

Remark 5.7
.

It seems less obvious that
the clean partite lemma also satisfies property
( )
‣
4.4

of Proposition
4.4
, meaning that if

{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{B}{F}_{m}
holds
for some natural number
m
, then
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{H}{F}_{m}
follows (provided that

{\mathscr{B}}_{F}
has clean intersections). We shall return to this
statement, which is central
to our ability to preserve odd girth, in
Corollary
6.3
below.

5.3.
The second partite
construction

The following strengthening of the induced Ramsey theorem was
proved independently
by Abramson and Harrington
[
1
]
,
and by Nešetřil and Rödl
[
21
]
.

Theorem 5.8
.

For all ordered graphs
F
and
B
and every number of colours
r

there exists an ordered graph
G
satisfying

G\longrightarrow(B)^{F}_{r}\,,

which means that for every colouring
\varphi\colon\binom{G}{F}\longrightarrow[r]
there exists
a copy
B^{\star}\in\binom{G}{B}
such that
\binom{B^{\star}}{F}

is monochromatic.∎

This result is sometimes expressed by saying that ordered
graphs form a Ramsey class
or a Ramsey category. We do not introduce the corresponding
abstract language here
and refer the interested reader to the preface of
[
29
]
.

By choosing
G
according to Theorem
5.8
and setting

{\mathscr{G}}_{F}=\binom{G}{F}

one sees that for every ordered
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
and
every number of colours
r

there exists an ordered
F
-system
{(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{F})}
such that
for every colouring

\varphi\colon{\mathscr{G}}_{F}\longrightarrow[r]
there is a semi-induced copy

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F})

of
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
such that
{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}
is monochromatic.
In several respects this is
weaker than Proposition
5.2
and thus we run
another partite construction,
this time with the clean partite lemma.
The advantage of horizontal clean intersections is most
clearly spelled out
in
[
29
]
*Lemma 4.7 and
[
29
]
*Lemma 4.14.
Here is a straightforward adaptation of the basic ideas to
our current situation.

Lemma 5.9
.

Suppose that
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
denotes a weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
for some
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
and that we have

(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})=(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F_{\bullet}})

for two pictures
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
,
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
over

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
and a partite
(\Pi^{F_{\bullet}},{\mathscr{P}}^{F_{\bullet}})
-conglomerate

(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}})
.
If
(\Pi,{\mathscr{P}}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}_{F})
and
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}},{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}})
are clean,
then so is
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})
.

Proof.

Again we need to check that
(\Sigma,{\mathscr{Q}}_{B},{\mathscr{Q}}_{F})

satisfies the three
clauses
( )
‣
5.1
–
( )
‣
5.1
of Definition
5.1
.
As usual, we denote the canonical projection from
\Sigma

to

by
\psi
.

Stage A:

Starting with
( )
‣
5.1
we consider two distinct copies

F_{\star},F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{Q}}_{F}
.
If
F_{\star},F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}}
we appeal to the
assumption that
{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}}
has clean
intersections. So we can assume

from now on, so that there is
a unique standard copy

of

with

First case:
F_{\star\star}\not\in{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}}

This means that there also exists a standard copy

with

If
\Pi_{\circ}=\Pi_{\circ\circ}

so we can assume

from now on,
which implies that the

and

immediately yields

If, on the other hand, the aforementioned copy

then (

) tells us

and our assertion follows from the fact that

has a

with each of
F_{\star}
,
F_{\star\star}
.

Second case:
F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{H}}_{{F_{\bullet}}}

If

we exploit that the copies in

{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ}_{F}

have clean intersections and otherwise property

‣
5.1

of

being clean yields

|V(F_{\star})\cap V(F_{\star\star})|\leq|V(\Pi_{\circ}^{F_{\bullet}})\cap V(F_{\star\star})|\leq 2\,.

Stage B:

Moving on to the verification of
( )
‣
5.1
we consider two

(B^{\star},{\mathscr{B}}_{F}^{\star})\in{\mathscr{Q}}_{B}
and

F_{\star\star}\in{\mathscr{Q}}_{F}\smallsetminus{\mathscr{B}}^{\star}_{F}
,
and need to show that the intersection of

and

is clean.
Let

be a standard copy
of

with

.
Since

is clean, only the case

is interesting. If

So it remains to discuss the case that some standard

satisfies

\Pi_{\circ}\neq\Pi_{\circ\circ}

and

.
Now we have

So if the graphs

,

we can exploit

‣

.

Stage C:

Finally addressing

‣
5.1
we consider two distinct copies

and

and

(\Pi_{\circ\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ\circ}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ\circ}_{F})
with

and

respectively. As usual, it suffices

, so that we have

If the intersection of
\Pi^{F_{\bullet}}_{\circ}
and

is clean,
everything is clear, and we can assume from now on that

is some copy

. As long as

that

In the remaining case,

occurs.
∎

We are now ready to describe the construction
\varUpsilon^{(1)}

promised at the beginning of this section.
As mentioned earlier, the proof is rendered
by a partite construction and parallels the proof of the clean partite
lemma—Proposition
5.6
. In fact, we shall use the
clean partite lemma
here. The other difference concerns the initial conglomerate

(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})

underlying the pictures in the construction. In the context
of Proposition
5.2

the conglomerate
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
will be provided by
Theorem
5.8

on Ramsey classes. As a result we have less control over the
structural properties
of
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
and this is reflected in the
conclusion of Proposition
5.2
.
In particular, the delivered conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})

falls short of preserving distances and odd girth.
These shortcomings will be addressed in
§
6
by another
application of the partite construction method.

Proof of Proposition
5.2
.

Given an ordered
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with clean
intersections and a
number of colours
r
we proceed as follows.

•

By Theorem
5.8
there exists an ordered graph
G

satisfying
G\longrightarrow(B)^{F}_{r}
.
Set

{\mathscr{G}}_{F}=\binom{G}{F}
, let

{\mathscr{G}}_{B}
be the collection of all semi-induced ordered
copies of
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})

in the ordered
F
-system
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
, and observe
that
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})

is an ordered weak
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate.
Choose an arbitrary enumeration
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}=\{F(1),\dots,F(N)\}
of
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
.

•

Starting with picture zero we recursively define a
sequence
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)_{\alpha\leq N}

of clean pictures over
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})
. If for
some
\alpha\in[N]

we have just constructed the
clean picture
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\bigr)
,
then we know that the copies of
F
belonging
to its constituent over
F(\alpha)
have clean intersections.
By Proposition
5.6
the clean partite lemma

\mathrm{CPL}_{r}(\cdot)

applied to this constituent yields a clean partite conglomerate

\bigl(H_{\alpha},{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}\bigr)
.
By Lemma
5.9
the picture

\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)=\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\bigr)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}\bigl(H_{\alpha},{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}\bigr)\,,

where the amalgamation occurs over
F(\alpha)
, is
clean again and, therefore,
our construction continues.

•

This recursive process culminates with a final
picture
\bigl(\Pi_{N},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F}\bigr)
.
We order the vertices of
\Pi_{N}
in such a manner that
each music line
becomes an interval and the ordering of these intervals
reflects the
vertex ordering of the ordered graph
G
. Since the copies
in
{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B}\cup{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F}
intersect each music
line at most once,
this ensures that these copies are ordered correctly in
\Pi_{N}
.
So we have converted
\bigl(\Pi_{N},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{N,F}\bigr)
into an
ordered
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate.

The partition relation
{\mathscr{P}}_{N,B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}

follows from the
same standard argument we have already presented in the proof of
Proposition
5.6
and
we omit the details.

It remains to address the preservation of the clique
number. To this end,
we prove
\omega(\Pi_{\alpha})=\omega(B)
by induction on
\alpha\leq N
.
The base case
\alpha=0
is trivial; in the induction step we
assume
\omega(\Pi_{\alpha-1})=\omega(B)
for some

\alpha\in[N]
and consider
a clique
K
in
\Pi_{\alpha}
. If
K
is completely
contained in
H_{\alpha}
, then
its order is at most

\omega(H_{\alpha})=\omega\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}\bigr)\leq\omega(\Pi_{\alpha-1})=\omega(B)

by Proposition
5.6
( )
‣
5.6
.

Otherwise there
are a standard
copy
\Pi^{\circ}_{\alpha-1}
of
\Pi_{\alpha-1}
and a
vertex
v
in
K
such that
v\in V(\Pi^{\circ}_{\alpha-1})\smallsetminus V(H_{\alpha})
.
Since
v
is
adjacent to all
other vertices of
K
, we have
K\subseteq\Pi^{\circ}_{\alpha-1}
and,
consequently, the order of
K
is at most

\omega(\Pi_{\alpha-1})=\omega(B)
.
This proves
\omega(\Pi_{\alpha})\leq\omega(B)
and the
reverse inequality is obvious.
∎

6.
Conform Ramsey conglomerates

For the proof of Proposition
2.6
we recall
that
\varUpsilon_{r}^{(1)}
from Proposition
5.2
already provides
a clean conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
preserving the

Consequently,

and

For the inductive step, we run a partite construction, where we employ

from

horizontally. Since the standard

Roughly speaking, the following picturesque statement rendered

Lemma 6.1
.

(

(

)

(

)

(

Proof.

‣

.
Now
xP^{\prime}uQ^{\prime\prime}vP^{\prime\prime\prime}y
is an
x
-
y
-walk in
\Pi_{\circ}
of at
most the same length as
P

and
F_{\star}\in\binom{\Pi_{\circ}}{F}_{n}
leads again to the
desired path. So we can assume

P^{\prime\prime}\not\subseteq H
in the sequel.

Suppose next that
u=x
and
v=y
. By
( )(0 )
the intersection of
F^{\prime}
and
{F_{\bullet}}
is
clean; as
\psi(x)
,
\psi(y)

belong to both graphs, we have
\psi(x)\psi(y)\in E(G)
.
Consequently,
xy

is an edge of
F_{\star}
and our claim is again clear.
So we can assume from now on that
P^{\prime\prime}
has length at most
n-1
.

By
{F_{\bullet}}\in\binom{G}{F}_{n-1}
applied to the

\psi(u)
-
\psi(v)
-walk
\psi[P^{\prime\prime}]
,
which is not contained in
{F_{\bullet}}
, there is a
\psi(u)
-
\psi(v)
-path

R^{\prime\prime}\subseteq{F_{\bullet}}
, which is shorter than
P^{\prime\prime}
. Now

\psi[xP^{\prime}u]R^{\prime\prime}\psi[vP^{\prime\prime\prime}y]

is a
\psi(x)
-
\psi(y)
-walk in
G
and shorter than
P
.
Due to
F^{\prime}\in{\mathscr{G}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{G}{F}_{n-1}

this entails that some
\psi(x)
-
\psi(y)
-path
S\subseteq F^{\prime}
is shorter
than
P
as well, wherefore the desired
x
-
y
-path

R\subseteq F_{\star}
exists again.

Having thereby proved
( )
‣
6.1
we proceed with
( )
‣
6.1
.
Assume towards a contradiction that
\Sigma
contains an odd
cycle
C
whose
length is at most
2n-1
. The projection
\psi
sends
C

to an odd closed walk
D

in
G
of the same length as
C
. Due to
\mathrm{og}(G)\geq 2n-1

this implies that both
C

and
D
are cycles of length
2n-1
. If
C
intersects
H

in at most one vertex,
then
C
has to be contained in a single standard copy of

\Pi
, contrary
to
\mathrm{og}(\Pi)\geq 2n+1
. Thus we can assume that
s=|V(C)\cap V(H)|
is at least
2
.
Consequently,
C
is of the form

(6.1)

C=x_{1}P_{1}\dots x_{s}P_{s}\,,

where
V(C)\cap V(H)=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{s}\}

and
P_{\varrho}
is an
x_{\varrho}
-
x_{\varrho+1}
-path for every

\varrho\in\mathds{Z}/s\mathds{Z}
.

Claim 6.2
.

If for some
\varrho\in\mathds{Z}/s\mathds{Z}
the length of
P_{\varrho}
is
at most
n-1
,
then this path is contained in
H
.

Proof.

Assume contrariwise that the length of
P_{\varrho}
is at
most
n-1
, while

P_{\varrho}\not\subseteq H
. Since
\psi
is injective on

V(C)
, the image

\psi[P_{\varrho}]
is a

\psi(x_{\varrho})
-
\psi(x_{\varrho+1})
-path in
G
. Together
with
\psi[P_{\varrho}]\not\subseteq{F_{\bullet}}
and
{F_{\bullet}}\in\binom{G}{F}_{n-1}
this shows
that there exists a

\psi(x_{\varrho})
-
\psi(x_{\varrho+1})
-path
Q\subseteq{F_{\bullet}}

whose length is strictly smaller than the length of
P_{\varrho}
. Both

Q\psi[x_{\varrho+1}P_{\varrho+1}\dots x_{\varrho}]\quad\text{ and }\quad\psi[x_{\varrho}P_{\varrho}x_{\varrho+1}]Q^{-1}\,,

where
Q^{-1}
denotes
Q
traversed in reverse order,
are closed walks in
G

whose lengths are at most
2n-2
. Moreover, the parities
of their lengths are different
and, therefore, one of them is odd. Thereby we reach a
contradiction to
\mathrm{og}(G)\geq 2n-1
.
∎

Since
\mathrm{og}(H)\geq 2n+1
implies
C\not\subseteq H
, it
follows that one of the paths

P_{1},\dots,P_{s}
has length at least
n
. This path needs
to be unique and the other
paths are contained in
H
. For these reasons we can
rewrite (
6.1
)
as
C=xPyQ
, where
x,y\in V(C)\cap V(H)
, the

x
-
y
-path
P
has no inner vertices
in
H
, and the
y
-
x
-path
Q\subseteq H
has length at
most
{n-1}
.
Clearly,
P
is completely contained in a single standard
copy
(\Pi_{\circ},{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ}_{B},{\mathscr{P}}^{\circ}_{F})
. As the
constituent of this picture
over
{F_{\bullet}}
is distance preserving in
H
, it contains an

x
-
y
-path
R
whose length
is at most the length of
Q
. Now

xRyQ\quad\text{ and }\quad xPyR^{-1}

are closed walks in
H
and
\Pi_{\circ}
, respectively, whose
lengths are at most
2n-1
.
Moreover, their parities are different, so that one of them
is odd. Thus we get a
contradiction either to
\mathrm{og}(H)\geq 2n+1
or to

\mathrm{og}(\Pi_{\circ})\geq 2n+1
.
∎

Keeping a promise made in Remark
5.7
we can now
easily deduce a further
property of the clean partite lemma.

Corollary 6.3
.

Let
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
be a partite
F
-system with clean
intersections. If for some
natural number
n
we have
{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{B}{F}_{n}
, then for
every number of colours
r
the clean
conglomerate
\mathrm{CPL}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})=(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})

satisfies
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{H}{F}_{n}
.

Proof.

This is clear for
n=1
, so we can assume
n\geq 2
from now
on. Let us recall that

(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
is obtained by means of a partite
construction. We keep using
the notation from the explanation of this construction
given immediately before
Proposition
5.6
.

Owing to the items
( )
‣
4.4
and
( )
‣
4.4
of
Proposition
4.4

we know
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{G}{F}_{n-1}
and that the
copies in
{\mathscr{G}}_{F}
have
clean intersections. We want to establish

{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\subseteq\binom{\Pi_{\alpha}}{F}_{n}
for
every non-negative integer

\alpha\leq N
by induction on
\alpha
. The case
\alpha=N

of this assertion
will then prove our corollary.

The base case
\alpha=0
is clear, because picture zero is
just a disjoint union
of copies of
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
and
{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{B}{F}_{n}
is assumed.
Suppose now that we already know

{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\subseteq\binom{\Pi_{\alpha-1}}{F}_{n}

for some
\alpha\in[N]
. Utilising
Proposition
4.4
one easily
checks that all assumptions of
Lemma
6.1
( )
‣
6.1
are satisfied
for the partite amalgamation

\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)=\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha-1,F}\bigr)\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}\bigl(H_{\alpha},{\mathscr{H}}_{\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{F(\alpha)}},{\mathscr{H}}_{F(\alpha)}\bigr)

and thus we have indeed
{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\subseteq\binom{\Pi_{\alpha}}{F}_{n}
.
∎

We conclude by establishing the following strengthening of
Proposition
2.6
.

Proposition 6.4
.

For every ordered graph
F
and every integer
n\geq 1

there exists a construction
\varUpsilon^{(n)}

which, given an ordered
F
-system
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with clean

{\mathscr{B}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{B}{F}_{n}
and a number of
colours
r
, yields
an ordered
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
\varUpsilon^{(n)}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})=(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})

such that

(
)

{\mathscr{H}}_{B}\longrightarrow(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})^{F}_{r}
,

(
)

(
0
)

{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\subseteq\binom{H}{F}_{n}
,

(
0
)

\omega(H)=\omega(B)
,

(
0
)

\mathrm{og}(H)\geq\min\{2n+1,\mathrm{og}(B)\}
,

(
)

and the
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate
(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
is clean.

Before proving Proposition
6.4
we note that it implies

2.6
. First we observe that the assumptions
of Proposition

are less restrictive. Indeed,
given an
n
-conform ordered

(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
, as assumed in

‣

and

‣

of Definition

ensure that

has clean intersections and

.

Concerning the conclusion of Proposition
6.4
, we note that
the ordered
(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
-conglomerate

\varUpsilon^{(n)}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})=(H,{\mathscr{H}}_{B},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
clearly

‣

of Proposition

.
Moreover, part

of Proposition

implies that

has clean

n

of

of Proposition

, follow directly from the

‣

of Proposition

combined with the assumption that

is

-conform itself.

Proof.

We argue by induction on

, using the construction

\varUpsilon^{(1)}
provided by

5.2
as a base case. Assuming now
that for some

we have the construction

at our disposal and that an

(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
with clean intersections

as well as a number of colours

are given, we perform

as in the proof of Proposition

, the only

vertically we use the conglomerate
(G,{\mathscr{G}}_{B},{\mathscr{G}}_{F})=\varUpsilon^{(n-1)}_{r}(B,{\mathscr{B}}_{F})
.
Again this yields a sequence
\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,B},{\mathscr{P}}_{\alpha,F}\bigr)_{\alpha\leq N}

of clean pictures and the last of them can be converted into a

-conglomerate, which we shall denote

In particular,

‣

of Proposition

.

The partition relation

‣

‣

Next, a straightforward induction on

. Now

for

.
∎

7.
Concluding remarks

7.1.
Generalisations of the main result

The first generalisation concerns the girth of the canonical Ramsey graph
H
in
Theorem
1.1
. It seems likely that, as long as
F
is not a forest,
Theorem
2.4
remains valid when we add the demand that
H
and
F

should have the same girth. In the non-canonical setting, such a result was obtained
recently by Reiher and Rödl. In fact,
the proof of their result provides
a system
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}
of copies of
F
in
H
, which itself contains
no short cycles (see
[
29
]
*§ 5), and we believe that those results
extend to the canonical setting.

The second generalisation concerns hypergraphs. The proof of Theorem
1.1

presented here can be partly extended to linear hypergraphs. For hypergraphs
the clique number is replaced by the size of the largest subset
X

of vertices such that any two vertices in
X
are contained in a hyperedge.
However, it is perhaps less clear what the analogous concepts of odd girth,

n
-inducedness, and distance preservation for such hypergraphs are.
It seems plausible that versions of
Theorems
1.1
and
2.4
hold for general hypergraphs.

The last generalisation we briefly mention concerns a common generalisation of
our result and Theorem
5.8
in the context of Ramsey classes, when we colour
arbitrary subgraphs. In that context an induced canonical Ramsey theorem
with maintained clique number was provided
by Prömel and Voigt
[
27
]
and it would be of some interest to establish
a result subsuming both their work and Theorem
2.4
.

7.2.
Classical versus canonical Ramsey theory

As it turned out, many results in Ramsey theory can be
paralleled in the canonical context.
For example, it follows from the work of
Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado
[
6
]
*§ 16.4 (see
also reference
[
9
]
*(4.2))
and of Shelah
[
34
]
that in terms of the number of exponentiations
the canonical Ramsey number and the non-canonical
Ramsey number (for at least four colours) for cliques in
hypergraphs display the same behaviour.
Another example, in the somewhat different context of random graphs,
concerns the threshold for the corresponding Ramsey
properties. For graph
cliques with at least four vertices those thresholds coincide,
which follows from the work of
Rödl and Ruciński
[
30
,
31
]

and of Kamčev and Schacht
[
18
]
.
A far-reaching generalisation of these parallel developments
would be an affirmative answer to the question of whether having the Ramsey property
for sufficiently many colours yields the canonical Ramsey property as well.
For graphs this naïve question reads as follows.

Question
.

Given an ordered graph
F
, does there exist an integer
r
such that
for every ordered graph
H
that satisfies the relation

H\longrightarrow(F)_{r}

we also have

H\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.3194pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\vphantom{f}\raisebox{-2.1pt}[0.0pt][0.0pt]{$\scriptstyle\cstar$}}}(F)
?

Note that for graphs
F
with at most two edges this question is trivial, since
any colouring of such small graphs is canonical.

More interestingly, by applying the machinery developed in
[
29
]
we
can answer this question in the negative when we replace
H

by a system
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}
of copies of an ordered graph
F
with at least three edges.
For such graphs there are at least five equivalence relations on
E(F)
and, hence,
at least one of them corresponds to a non-canonical colouring. We fix such
a non-canonical equivalence relation,
say
\equiv^{F}
, and let
r\in\mathds{N}
be given.

With the notation developed in
[
29
]
the pair
(F,\equiv^{F})
is a pretrain
and
[
29
]
*Proposition 9.1 applied to
(F,\equiv^{F})
and
r
yields
a pretrain system
(H,\equiv^{H},{\mathscr{H}}_{F})
with the Ramsey property

{\mathscr{H}}_{F}\longrightarrow(F)_{r}
. Moreover, the restriction of
\equiv^{H}
to copies of
F
in
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}
is identical to
\equiv^{F}
. So, we can colour
E(H)

in such a way that no copy of
F
from
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}
is canonically coloured.

Consequently, the version of the question for the system
{\mathscr{H}}_{F}

has the expected negative answer.
Moreover, if
F=K_{k}
for some
k\geq 3
(and for certain other graphs
F
), the
constructions involved in the proof of
[
29
]
*Proposition 9.1
yield
{\mathscr{H}}_{K_{k}}=\binom{H}{K_{k}}
. This answers the question posed above
negatively for such instances.

Nevertheless, in light of the discussion above one may wonder whether these parallel
developments in canonical and non-canonical Ramsey theory are just anecdotal
or whether there is some profound connection.
